title: It is finished (John 19:25–30)
hook: his mother, the beloved disciple, I thirst, and it is finished
carry: a debt paid, a victory won

segments.voice: Yesterday, a coat with no seam, like the one Josephus described, and soldiers casting lots. Your line: woven from the top.

While the soldiers gamble, a few people stand near the cross. John names them. His mother. His mother's sister. Mary the wife of Cleophas. Mary Magdalene. And the disciple whom Jesus loved. The other men who followed him are nowhere in John's scene. These few stayed. And from the cross, with the little breath he has left, Jesus speaks to them. In John's Gospel, he says only three things from the cross.

The first is to his mother and his friend. In the King James Bible: "Woman, behold thy son!" And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother!" From that hour, John says, that disciple took her to his own home. Dying, he makes sure his mother has a home. Christians read it in more than one way. Read plainly, it's simple, faithful care. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also hear Mary given as mother to the church, with the beloved disciple standing for every follower. The second: "I thirst." The man who offered a woman at a well living water, and said whoever believes in him will never thirst, is thirsty. Someone lifts a sponge of sour wine to him on a branch of hyssop, the plant used at the first Passover to mark the doorposts. Then the third. "When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost." In Greek, it is finished is one word: tetelestai. It comes from telos, the end, the goal, the point something has been moving toward. It doesn't mean it's over, I'm done for. It means complete, accomplished, brought to its goal. Just before, John uses the same verb: Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished. Christians hear this one word as the heart of what they believe the cross achieved, and churches describe that in different words: a debt paid, a victory won, love shown to the end. Each reading hears completion, not defeat. Then: he bowed his head. John makes it sound like a choice. He handed over his spirit.

Think of one small thing you've left half done, a text never sent, a drawer half sorted, a thank-you note, and picture yourself completing it and then stopping: not grabbing the next thing, just resting in done. If you pray, offer that small completion to God; if not, simply notice how good finished feels.
Tetelestai. One word in Greek for it is finished: not it's over, but it's complete, brought to its goal.
Your line: a debt paid, a victory won. Or, as others say it, love shown to the end. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Good Friday many churches hold services around Jesus's last words from the cross, sometimes called the Seven Last Words, gathered from all four Gospels; three of them come from John.

original.note: Greek: it is finished, it stands complete. from telos, the end or goal. one word in Greek.

trapdoor: what it means: it's complete. the work he came to do is brought to its goal.
what a scholar hears: tetelestai, a perfect tense from telos, echoing 19:28's 'all things were now accomplished', the same verb twice in three verses.

chat.says: When Jesus said It is finished, did he mean he'd given up?
options: No. Tetelestai means complete, accomplished, brought to its goal.
Yes. It means it's over, I'm done for: a cry of defeat at the end.
No. It means the soldiers were done dividing up his clothes by lot.
chat.meaning: Tetelestai comes from telos, the goal. It means complete, accomplished; Christians hear completion, not defeat.

tetelestai.meaning: Greek for it is finished: complete, accomplished

telos.meaning: Greek for the end, the goal

hyssop.meaning: the plant used at the first Passover to mark doorposts

Cleophas.meaning: husband of one of the Marys near the cross

Mary Magdalene.meaning: one of the few women who stayed near the cross
